questions.q: Which statement about JavaScript on one thread is right?
questions.explain: Concurrency is many jobs in progress; parallelism is many executing at once. Your callbacks run one at a time, but while one request waits on the network, others can be started. Parallel JavaScript needs worker threads.
options: It runs several of your callbacks at the same instant on different cores
It is concurrent: many jobs can be in progress, taking turns on the thread while their waiting overlaps outside it
It can only have one network request in progress at a time
It is parallel, because promises run on background threads

questions.q: Resizing 200 product photos is pure computation. Why does running the resizes with Promise.all not make it faster?
questions.explain: Async concurrency overlaps waiting. Computation still needs the thread. To use several cores, move the work to worker threads.
options: The work is CPU-bound on the single JavaScript thread, so the jobs still run one after another; concurrency only helps when jobs spend time waiting
Promise.all runs them in reverse order
It is faster, by a factor of 200

questions.q: Which is not a reason to limit how many jobs run at once?
questions.explain: JavaScript can start as many promises as you like. The limits come from the other side (connections, rate limits) and from your own resources (memory).
options: The email provider refuses more than 5 connections
The database pool has only 10 connections
Each job holds a large file in memory
JavaScript cannot start more than 5 promises at a time

questions.q: Why does a pool with limit 5 usually finish sooner than batches of 5?
questions.explain: Both respect the limit. The pool keeps all slots busy; batches leave slots idle while the slowest job of each batch finishes.
options: The pool runs more than 5 jobs at once
A pool starts a new job as soon as any slot frees up; a batch waits for its slowest job before starting any new one
Batches run their jobs one at a time

questions.explain: Jobs finish in time order, but each result is stored at its item's index, so the output keeps the input order, like Promise.all.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Four workers each run one job at a time, so at most four jobs are in progress at any moment.

questions.q: In the pool, two workers finish at the same moment and both run const index = next++. Can they get the same index?
questions.explain: Two callbacks never run at the same instant on one thread. Races in JavaScript happen across awaits, not inside synchronous lines.
options: Yes, so a lock is needed around that line
No: the line is synchronous and JavaScript runs one callback at a time, so one worker's read-and-increment always completes before the other's
No, because next++ is atomic in all languages

questions.q: What would a pool with limit = 0 do if it did not check its limit?
questions.explain: With no workers, Promise.all([]) resolves at once and no job ever runs: a silent failure. That is why the pool rejects a limit below 1 with its own RangeError.
options: Run jobs one at a time
Start no workers and resolve with an array of empty slots, without running any job

questions.q: In the lesson's pool, job 3 fails while job 4 is running. What happens?
questions.explain: The failed flag stops workers from taking new items. Job 4 cannot be stopped without cancellation, so it runs to the end; its result is ignored.
options: Job 4 is cancelled and jobs 5 onwards run
The pool rejects with job 3's error, job 4 finishes on its own, and no new jobs start
The pool ignores the error and continues

questions.q: When do you need a limiter (like p-limit) rather than mapWithLimit?
questions.explain: A limiter queues each job as it arrives and starts it when a slot is free. mapWithLimit needs the whole list at the start.
options: When the list of jobs is known up front
When jobs arrive over time from different callers but must share one limit, for example all requests calling one payment API
When you want results in input order

questions.q: Why are cancellation's two roles split into AbortController and AbortSignal?
questions.explain: Passing only the signal down means a called function cannot cancel work that belongs to its caller.
options: The code that may cancel keeps the controller; the work only receives the signal, so it can observe cancellation but not trigger it
The controller is for timers and the signal for fetch

questions.explain: Without a reason, the signal's reason is a DOMException named AbortError. throwIfAborted() throws that exact reason object.

questions.q: Why should code check error.name === "AbortError" rather than the error's message?
questions.explain: Node says "This operation was aborted", browsers say something else. The name (AbortError, TimeoutError) is the portable way to recognise the kind of error.
options: The default messages differ between Node.js and browsers; the name is standard

questions.q: A cancellable sleep(ms, { signal }) finishes normally. Which clean-up step must it still do?
questions.explain: A listener added with addEventListener stays until it fires or is removed. { once: true } only removes it after it fires. A signal that lives for a whole campaign would collect thousands of listeners.
options: Remove its abort listener from the signal, or every call leaves a listener behind on a long-lived signal
Nothing, listeners remove themselves when a promise resolves

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The abort after 10 ms clears the 5-second timer and rejects with the reason, so the sleep ends early and nothing keeps running.

questions.q: What does AbortSignal.timeout(3000) give you?
questions.explain: It is a ready-made signal; pass it to fetch or any function that accepts a signal. Its reason's name is "TimeoutError", so you can tell a timeout from a user cancel.
options: A controller that aborts after 3 seconds
A signal that aborts by itself after 3 seconds, with a reason named TimeoutError
A promise that rejects after 3 seconds
A function that times out any promise

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: AbortSignal.any aborts as soon as any of its signals aborts, taking that signal's reason. The user aborted first.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A fetch given an already-aborted signal rejects immediately with the signal's reason, an AbortError by default. Without the abort it would print in stock.

questions.q: A request handler aborts its database query when the client disconnects. What else should happen for cancellation to be complete?
questions.explain: Cancellation that stops at the first layer only hides the waste: the calls further down keep running. Pass the signal all the way down.
options: The signal should be passed on to every call the handler makes (fetches, other services), and those should stop their work too

questions.q: What is a race condition?
questions.explain: In async JavaScript, operations overlap across awaits. If the outcome changes with which one finishes first, that is a race condition.
options: A bug where the result depends on the timing of operations that overlap
A function that runs too fast
An error thrown by the event loop

questions.q: Earlier searches are slower. What does this print?
questions.explain: The answer for "rice 5kg" arrives at 15 ms and is shown, then the slower answer for "ric" arrives at 40 ms and overwrites it. This is the stale-response race.
options: results for ric, results for rice 5kg

questions.q: Which fix for stale search results also saves work on the server?
questions.explain: Ignoring stale answers fixes the display. Aborting also closes the old request, so neither side keeps working on it. Combine both, because some APIs cannot be cancelled.
options: Only ignoring answers whose query is not the latest
Aborting the previous request when a new search starts (and still ignoring any old answer that slips through)
Adding a setTimeout before showing results

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Both checks ran before either booking was written, so both passed: check-then-act. Both customers were told "booked", and Bola's write overwrote Ada's.

questions.q: A wallet service runs on four server processes. Why is an in-process mutex not enough to stop double withdrawals?
questions.explain: An in-process lock only coordinates code in one process. Shared state in a database needs the database's guarantees, or a distributed lock.
options: Mutexes do not work with async functions
Each process has its own mutex, so two requests handled by different processes do not wait for each other; the database must enforce the rule (a transaction with a lock or a conditional update)
The mutex makes withdrawals too slow

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: B waits for A to finish. A fails, but last = result.catch(() => {}) keeps the chain going, so B still runs. Without that catch, one failed job would block every later job.

questions.q: A price is cached for a minute. When the cache expires, 200 requests arrive at once and all query the database. What is this, and what is the fix?
questions.explain: Request coalescing ("single flight") lets the first caller start the lookup and makes later callers await the same promise, so 200 requests cause one query.
options: A cache stampede; coalesce requests by sharing the in-flight promise for the same key
A memory leak; clear the cache
A stale response; abort old requests

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The first two rice calls share one query; oil has its own: 2. After they finish, finally removes the entries, so the last rice call starts a new query: 3.

questions.q: Why does the coalescing map delete its entry in finally, not only after success?
questions.explain: If a failed promise stayed in the map, every later caller would receive that same failure. Removing it either way makes the map hold only lookups that are still in progress.
options: So a failed lookup is not cached forever: the next caller retries instead of getting the same rejection again
So the value is cached for longer

questions.q: How can a test make a stale-response bug happen every time instead of occasionally?
questions.explain: When the test controls when each fake request completes, the problematic order is forced deterministically, and the fix can be proven.
options: Use deferred promises (Promise.withResolvers) for the fake requests and resolve them in the order the test chooses

questions.q: Should a cancelled search be logged as an error?
questions.explain: Logging normal cancellations as errors floods the logs and hides real failures. Check signal.aborted or the error's name first.
options: Yes, every rejection is an error
No: cancellation is expected behaviour; recognise it (by the signal or error name) and do not report it as a failure

questions.q: Finish mapWithLimit(items, limit, fn): run at most limit calls of fn at once, start the next one as soon as any finishes, and return the results in input order.
questions.explain: Start limit workers that each take the next index and await its job in a loop. Storing results by index keeps the input order.

questions.q: Finish sleep(ms, { signal }): reject at once with signal.reason if already aborted; on abort, clear the timer and reject with the reason; on normal completion, remove the listener and resolve.
questions.explain: The three cases are the three rules of a cancellable function: finish normally and clean up, stop on abort, and fail at once if already aborted.
questions.expected:
short sleep finished
long sleep: stopped by Ada
already aborted: stopped by Ada

questions.q: Fix onType so an older, slower answer can never overwrite a newer one: give each call an increasing id and only show the result if it is still the latest call.
questions.explain: Each call remembers its own id. After the await, a newer call may have started; comparing with latest drops the stale answer.

questions.q: Finish createMutex() so that exclusive(job) runs jobs one at a time in arrival order, and a failed job does not block the next. The two withdrawals must no longer both succeed.
questions.explain: Chaining each job onto the previous one serialises them, so the second withdrawal reads the balance after the first has written it. The catch keeps the chain alive after a failure.

questions.q: Finish loadStock(sku, signal) so it passes a signal to slowWarehouse that aborts when the caller's signal aborts or after 30 ms. Report a timeout as timeout and a user cancel as cancelled: REASON.
questions.explain: AbortSignal.any combines the caller's signal with a timeout signal. The reason tells you which one fired: a TimeoutError, or the caller's own reason.

questions.q: Finish getRate(currency) so that concurrent calls for the same currency share one lookup, and the entry is removed when the lookup ends.
questions.explain: The first caller for a key stores the promise; later callers get the same promise. finally removes it when done, so the map only holds lookups in progress.

questions.q: Add a signal option to the pool: each worker must call signal?.throwIfAborted() before taking the next item, so aborting stops new jobs. The campaign is stopped after the first few emails.
questions.explain: Checking the signal before each new job makes the pool stop starting work as soon as the campaign is aborted, and the pool rejects with the abort reason.
questions.expected: stopped: wrong price | sent fewer than 10: true
